entities.name: Royal Society and Scientific Societies
entities.label: Movement
entities.summary:
The Royal Society of London (founded 1660) and parallel scientific academies across Europe—including the Académie des Sciences (Paris, 1666) and the Berlin Academy (1700)—institutionalized the scientific method and transformed knowledge production. These societies established peer review, experimental replication, and collaborative research as epistemic norms, replacing solitary scholasticism with networked inquiry.

They published journals (*Philosophical Transactions*, 1665), archived observations, and standardized nomenclature across disciplines. By linking natural philosophy to practical applications—navigation, engineering, medicine—they bridged theory and craft, elevating empiricism as the arbiter of truth. Their legacy: the modern research community, the scientific paper, and the principle that knowledge advances through public scrutiny and reproducible evidence.
